title: Choosing a broker
problem: Billing, analytics and a new fraud model all need the order events, one of them wants last month's replayed, and the team put everything on one work queue.
summary: Brokers are logs or queues underneath. Kafka and Pulsar keep records and let readers replay; RabbitMQ and SQS route, acknowledge and delete each message; SNS fans out. Replay and many readers want a log, per-message routing wants a queue.
catTip: The newspaper archive lets me read any day I like, as often as I like. The post office hands each letter to one cat and it is gone. I pick the archive for history and the post office for errands. Never the other way round.

recall.q: What single question decides between a log broker and a queue broker?
recall.a: Whether more than one consumer needs the same events, or anyone will replay them: if so, a log such as Kafka. If each message is routed by content and consumed once by competing workers with per-message acks, a queue such as RabbitMQ or SQS, with SNS for fan-out.

guide.breaks: A queue used as an event bus copies every event into every consumer's queue and can never replay, while a log used as a work queue gives head-of-line blocking per partition and no per-message retry.
guide.tradeoffs: Logs give replay and fan-out but order only per partition and offer no per-message routing; queues route and retry each message but delete it on acknowledgement; managed services remove operations at the price of regional throughput ceilings.
guide.explainSimply: A log is a newspaper archive: every issue stays on the shelf and any reader can start from any date. A queue is a post office: each letter goes to one carrier and is gone once signed for. Pick the archive when many people need the same history, the post office when each item is an errand for one person.
guide.hint: Think about who else needs the same message, and whether anyone will ever ask for it again.

meow: Many readers or a replay? Log, meow. One worker, one ack, one retry? Queue. Nobody on call? Let the cloud hold the queue.

quiz.prompt: A food-delivery platform wants order events consumed by billing, analytics, notifications and a fraud model, and wants to replay last month's orders into a new model. Which broker shape fits?
options: A RabbitMQ queue with four competing consumers
An SQS standard queue with a long visibility timeout
A partitioned log such as Kafka: each team reads with its own consumer group and resets offsets to replay
An SNS topic alone, since it fans out to every subscriber
quiz.explanation: Several independent readers plus replay is the log's defining case: consumer groups read the same bytes and offsets can be reset. SNS is the strongest distractor because it does fan out, but it keeps nothing, so a subscriber that was not there last month cannot replay it.

quiz.prompt: An SQS consumer takes 90 seconds to process a message and the queue uses the default visibility timeout. What happens?
options: Nothing; SQS waits until the consumer deletes the message
After 30 seconds the message becomes visible again and another consumer processes it too
The message is moved to the dead-letter queue after 30 seconds
SQS extends the timeout automatically while the consumer stays connected
quiz.explanation: The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds, after which an undeleted message reappears, which is how SQS implements at-least-once delivery. The dead-letter option is the plausible error: a message moves there only after maxReceiveCount receives under a redrive policy, not on a single timeout.

cards.q: Why does an SQS FIFO queue have a throughput ceiling that a standard queue does not?
cards.a: Ordering within a message group forces serialisation through one partition: 300 transactions per second per API action per partition, 3,000 with batches of ten. High-throughput mode spreads message groups over more partitions; a standard queue never orders, so it never serialises.

cards.q: RabbitMQ and Kafka both deliver in order. How do their ordering promises differ?
cards.a: RabbitMQ keeps a queue in publication order, but with several consumers on one queue each sees only its share, so a redelivery can reach a consumer after a newer message. Kafka orders within a partition and gives each partition to exactly one consumer in a group, so per-key order holds end to end.

glossary.note: The open messaging protocol RabbitMQ implements (version 0-9-1): publishers send to exchanges, which route to queues through bindings.
AWS's managed queue: consumers poll, a received message is hidden for the visibility timeout, and it is deleted only when the consumer says so.
AWS's managed pub/sub topic that pushes each message to every subscription, such as SQS queues, Lambda functions or HTTP endpoints.
